content: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory condition that affects the airways, commonly seen in both adults and children. It is characterized by symptoms such as wheezing, shortness of breath, chest tightness, and coughing. Managing asthma effectively often requires a collaborative approach between the patient and healthcare provider, known as shared decision-making (SDM). This process involves both parties exchanging information, including the patient’s values and preferences, to reach a consensus on the most appropriate treatment plan. SDM aims to empower patients to take an active role in managing their condition, potentially improving clinical outcomes and quality of life. The objective of this review was to evaluate the benefits and potential risks of SDM for adults and children with asthma. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, as well as clinical trial registries. The search was last updated on November 29, 2016. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared SDM interventions with control interventions, such as usual care or minimal interventions. Studies targeting healthcare professionals, patients, their families, or caregivers were included, provided the intervention focused on SDM. Studies with additional components beyond SDM were excluded unless the control group also received these components. Four RCTs were included in the review, involving a total of 1,342 participants. Three studies focused on children with asthma and their caregivers, while one study involved adults with asthma. The trials were conducted in the United States and the Netherlands, with durations ranging from 6 to 24 months. In one trial, the SDM intervention was delivered to healthcare providers, while in the other three, it was delivered directly to participants. Two pediatric studies utilized an online portal followed by face-to-face consultations. Another study combined face-to-face consultations with telephone calls, and the final study involved a seminar program for pediatric general practice physicians to promote SDM principles. All trials were open-label, though one study claimed participants were unaware of their physicians’ involvement in the trial. The review identified several methodological concerns, including selection bias, attrition bias, and selective reporting. One study notably under-recruited participants. The studies used varying methods to measure adherence to the intervention and reported outcomes inconsistently. In terms of results, one study involving adults with poorly controlled asthma reported improved quality of life in the SDM group compared to the control group, as measured by the Asthma Quality of Life Questionnaire (AQLQ) (mean difference 1.90, 95% confidence interval 1.24 to 2.91). However, two other trials did not find a similar benefit. Patient and parent satisfaction with pediatricians was higher in the SDM group in one trial involving children. Medication adherence was better in the SDM group in two studies—one involving adults and one involving children. For example, in one study, the mean number of controlled medication prescriptions over 26 weeks was 1.1 in the SDM group compared to 0.7 in the control group. Asthma-related healthcare visit rates were lower in the SDM group in one study (1.0 visits per year versus 1.4 visits per year; P = 0.016), but two other studies did not report differences in exacerbations or short courses of oral steroid prescriptions. One study reported better odds of participants in the SDM group experiencing no asthma problems compared to the usual care group (odds ratio 1.90, 95% confidence interval 1.26 to 2.87), but two other studies did not find improvements in asthma control with SDM. The review found no data on the acceptability of the intervention to healthcare professionals or on adverse events. Overall, the confidence in the results of the included studies ranged from very low to moderate, with downgrades due to risk of bias, imprecision, and indirectness. The authors concluded that the substantial differences between the four included RCTs prevent meaningful overall conclusions. While individual studies demonstrated some benefits of SDM, such as improved quality of life, higher patient and parent satisfaction, better medication adherence, fewer asthma-related healthcare visits, and improved asthma control, the evidence is limited and inconsistent. Future trials should be adequately powered and of sufficient duration to detect meaningful differences in outcomes such as exacerbations and hospitalizations. The use of standardized asthma outcome measures and validated scales would facilitate meta-analyses. Additionally, studies conducted in lower-income settings, including economic evaluations, and those involving adolescents, are needed. Systematic recording of adverse events and measurement of intervention fidelity are also recommended for future research.
